JESUS AS MESSIAH (HIGHER LEVEL) - STUDY NOTES

Note: this is a short chapter in the textbook. These notes cover everything in it. The topic is also looked at in Section H (The Bible: Literature and Sacred Text) and Section C (World Religions).

OPENING QUOTE
- The chapter opens with a quote from Kahlil Gibran about giving.
- Some people give a little of the much they have, and they give it for recognition. Their hidden desire makes their gifts ‘unwholesome’.
- Others have little and give it all. ‘These are the believers in life and the bounty of life, and their coffer is never empty.’
- Link to the chapter: Jesus’ idea of messiah is about giving everything - a life of love and service, ending in death.

KEY TERMS
- Messiah: means ‘anointed one’. A person chosen by God and recognised by those who are faithful to God.
- Davidic messiah: a messiah like a new King David, who would begin a new era in Jewish history and free the Jews from the Romans.
- Prophetic messiah: the messiah the Pharisees hoped for. He would fulfil the scriptures and free God’s people from oppression, as Moses freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt.
- Priestly messiah: the messiah the Essenes (Qumran) hoped for. He would bring a great war where God’s enemies would be defeated. Linked to Aaron and the tribe of Levi (the priests of the Temple).
- Jesus of history / Christ of faith: the debate about what we can know about the real, historical Jesus, given that the gospels were written after the Resurrection. Some commentators prefer the terms ‘Pre-Easter Jesus’ and ‘Post-Easter Jesus’.

BACKGROUND: ISRAEL AS GOD’S CHOSEN PEOPLE
- All through their history the people of Israel believed they were God’s chosen people.
- Through Abraham they made a covenant with God.
- This covenant was renewed and affirmed through Moses.
- God called the people to live by a strict moral code, underpinned by love of God.
- They believed God loved them and would care for them.

THE IDEA OF A MESSIAH
- The idea of a messiah is found all through the Old Testament.
- In times of difficulty the Jewish people found hope by looking forward to a messiah.
- When they suffered exile, oppression and slavery, they believed God would send a messiah to save them.
- ‘Messiah’ means ‘anointed one’.
- The messiah is chosen by God and recognised by those faithful to God.
- Different religious and social groups within Judaism at the time of Jesus understood the messiah in different ways.
- The idea of messiah as ‘anointed one’ was NOT the central image of messiah in first-century Palestine.

WHAT FIRST-CENTURY JEWS EXPECTED
- Jesus was not the messiah the people of the first century were hoping for or expecting.
- Jews in first-century Palestine hoped and prayed for a messiah to deliver (free) them from the pagan Romans.
- There was a general expectation that the messiah would be like a new King David.
- He would herald (announce, begin) a new era in Jewish history.
- This vision is called the DAVIDIC MESSIAH.

JESUS’ NEW INTERPRETATION
- Jesus brought a new, alternative meaning of ‘messiah’.
- For Jesus, the messiah is one who ushers in (brings in) the Kingdom of God through:
- a life of love
- a life of service
- and eventual death.

THREE MESSIANIC EXPECTATIONS (SUMMARY)
- 1. Davidic messiah - general popular hope: a new King David, a new era, freedom from Rome.
- 2. Prophetic messiah - the Pharisees.
- 3. Priestly messiah - the Essenes at Qumran.

THE PHARISEES AND THE PROPHETIC MESSIAH
- The Pharisees looked forward to a future messiah whom God would send.
- He would deliver them from Roman rule.
- He would restore the Kingdom of God among the people of Israel.
- This PROPHETIC MESSIAH would fulfil the scriptures.
- He would liberate the people of God from oppression, just as Moses had freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt.

THE ESSENES AND THE PRIESTLY MESSIAH
- The Essenes were associated with the community at Qumran.
- They also looked forward to the coming of a messiah.
- They had a more exclusive and extreme outlook.
- They looked for a messiah who would herald a great war.
- In this war, those against God would be vanquished (defeated).
- Those loyal to God (meaning all those in the sect) would be vindicated (shown to be right).
- This vision is called the PRIESTLY MESSIAH.
- This messiah would be associated with Aaron and the tribe of Levi - the priests of the Temple.

JESUS’ AWARENESS OF MESSIANIC EXPECTATIONS
- Jesus would have been aware of the hopes and expectations of the people of Israel, especially the Jewish people settled in Palestine.
- In his preaching, teaching and living he announced the Kingdom of God.
- He showed he was aware of himself as the Messiah in the sense of the one who heralded this kingdom.

EVIDENCE 1: THE WOMAN AT THE WELL (JOHN 4:25-26)
- Jesus talks with a woman at a well, and his identity as Messiah comes up.
- The woman says: ‘I know that Messiah is coming…. When he comes he will proclaim all things to us.’
- Jesus says: ‘I am he, the one who is speaking to you.’
- Here Jesus openly identifies himself as the Messiah.

EVIDENCE 2: JESUS’ ACTIONS
- Jesus’ actions also show he was aware of Jewish expectations about the Messiah.
- His acts of healing, love and compassion all show this.

EVIDENCE 3: THE ANOINTING AT BETHANY (MARK 14:3)
- Jesus is at Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, sitting at table.
- An unnamed woman comes with an alabaster jar of very costly ointment of nard.
- She breaks open the jar and pours the ointment on his head.
- By anointing him she is recognising him as the Messiah (the ‘anointed one’).
- Some people present criticise what she did.
- Jesus defends her (Mark 14:8-9): ‘She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for its burial. Truly I tell you, wherever the good news is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in remembrance of her.’
- Note: Jesus links the anointing to his burial - his idea of messiah includes death.

THE JESUS OF HISTORY AND THE CHRIST OF FAITH
- How far Jesus was aware of himself as the Messiah (‘anointed one’) has been discussed by scripture scholars for some time.
- This opens the debate about the relationship between the ‘Jesus of history’ and the ‘Christ of faith’.
- Some commentators prefer the terms ‘Pre-Easter Jesus’ and ‘Post-Easter Jesus’.
- The issue: what can we know about the historical Jesus, since all the gospels and New Testament accounts were written after the Resurrection (‘post-Easter’)?
- Question raised: to what extent did the experience of the Resurrection and the early Christian community ‘colour’ the evangelists’ view of the historical Jesus?

JESUS AND THE THREE EXPECTATIONS
- Jesus seems to have been particularly anxious NOT to identify himself, or be identified, with the priestly or Davidic ideas of messiah.
- Where Jesus does show some affinity (closeness) with the prophetic messiah, his idea of the Kingdom of God is very different from the Jewish expectation of the prophetic messiah.

WHY JESUS WAS RELUCTANT TO BE CALLED MESSIAH
- The first century was a highly politicised atmosphere. Expectations about the Messiah were very political.
- If Jesus had taken on that role, he would have had two choices:
- abandon his own more inclusive understanding of the hopes of Israel, OR
- be rejected as an impostor.
- This is because his agenda was not that of a political liberator, as many of his co-religionists (fellow Jews) imagined.
- All the Gospels, in different ways, show Jesus’ reluctance to be thought of simply in the messianic role.
- This reluctance shows when other people typecast him as messiah - whether his disciples or his religious and political opponents.

JESUS TEACHES WHAT KIND OF MESSIAH HE IS (MARK 8:31)
- There are several incidents in the gospels where Jesus seems to identify himself as the Messiah.
- But he was anxious that this was not misunderstood by his followers.
- Mark 8:31: ‘Then he began to teach them that he the Son of Man must undergo great suffering, and be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise again. He said all this quite openly.’
- Key points: Jesus calls himself ‘Son of Man’; he speaks of suffering, rejection by the elders, chief priests and scribes, death, and rising after three days.
- This is a suffering messiah - very different from the political, warrior or kingly messiah people expected.

TEXTBOOK ASSIGNMENTS AND QUESTION (USEFUL FOR EXAM PRACTICE)
- Essay: Messiah as understood by a first-century Jew - explore the three distinct messianic expectations; comment on Jesus’ awareness of them; explore the understanding of Jesus as a messianic figure.
- Explain the relationship between the ‘Jesus of history’ and the ‘Christ of faith’.
- Question: How aware was Jesus of the messianic expectations of his fellow Israelites?
- Group work: brainstorm the idea of messiah. What kinds of people are considered messiahs or saviours in today’s world?

QUICK REVISION CHECKLIST
- Messiah = anointed one.
- Davidic = new King David, new era, freedom from Rome (general expectation).
- Prophetic = Pharisees, fulfil scriptures, liberate like Moses.
- Priestly = Essenes/Qumran, great war, Aaron and tribe of Levi.
- Jesus: Kingdom of God through love, service and death.
- John 4:25-26 woman at the well: ‘I am he’.
- Mark 14:3-9 anointing at Bethany, house of Simon the leper, alabaster jar, nard.
- Mark 8:31 Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and rise after three days.
- Jesus of history vs Christ of faith / Pre-Easter vs Post-Easter Jesus.

rows.prompt: What does ‘messiah’ mean, and why did the Jewish people look forward to a messiah?
rows.model_answer: Messiah means ‘anointed one’, a person chosen by God and recognised by those faithful to God. In times of difficulty, such as exile, oppression and slavery, the Jewish people found hope in looking forward to a messiah whom God would send to save them.

rows.prompt: Name the three messianic expectations in first-century Judaism and the group linked to two of them.
rows.model_answer: The three were the Davidic messiah, the prophetic messiah and the priestly messiah. The Pharisees looked for a prophetic messiah, and the Essenes at Qumran looked for a priestly messiah. The Davidic messiah, a new King David, was the general popular expectation.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words what the Davidic messiah was.
rows.model_answer: The Davidic messiah was the general hope of first-century Jews for a messiah like a new King David. He would deliver them from the pagan Romans and herald a new era in Jewish history.

rows.prompt: Explain what the Pharisees hoped the messiah would do.
rows.model_answer: The Pharisees hoped God would send a messiah to deliver them from Roman rule and restore the Kingdom of God among the people of Israel. This prophetic messiah would fulfil the scriptures and free God’s people from oppression, just as Moses freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt.

rows.prompt: Describe the priestly messiah that the Essenes expected.
rows.model_answer: The Essenes at Qumran had an exclusive and extreme outlook. They expected a messiah who would herald a great war in which those against God would be vanquished and those loyal to God, the members of their sect, would be vindicated. This messiah was associated with Aaron and the tribe of Levi, the Temple priests.

rows.prompt: Describe the anointing at Bethany and explain its link to Jesus as Messiah.
rows.model_answer: In Mark 14:3, at the house of Simon the leper in Bethany, an unnamed woman broke an alabaster jar of costly nard and poured it on Jesus’ head. By anointing him she recognised him as the Messiah, the ‘anointed one’. When people criticised her, Jesus defended her and said she had anointed his body beforehand for burial.

rows.prompt: Explain the debate about the ‘Jesus of history’ and the ‘Christ of faith’.
rows.model_answer: All the gospels were written after the Resurrection, so scholars ask what we can really know about the historical Jesus. The question is how far the Resurrection experience and the early Christian community ‘coloured’ the evangelists’ view of Jesus. Some commentators call this the ‘Pre-Easter Jesus’ and the ‘Post-Easter Jesus’.

rows.prompt: Why was Jesus reluctant to be called the Messiah?
rows.model_answer: In the highly political atmosphere of the first century, the Messiah was expected to be a political liberator. If Jesus took that role he would have had to abandon his more inclusive vision of Israel’s hopes or be rejected as an impostor. So he avoided being typecast by disciples or opponents, and taught that the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and rise (Mark 8:31).

rows.prompt: (a) Outline the three messianic expectations that existed among Jewish people at the time of Jesus. (b) Explain how Jesus’ understanding of messiah differed from these expectations.
rows.model_answer:
(a) At the time of Jesus there were three main messianic expectations. First, the general popular hope was for a Davidic messiah, a new King David who would deliver the Jews from the pagan Romans and herald a new era in Jewish history. Second, the Pharisees looked for a prophetic messiah sent by God to deliver them from Roman rule and restore the Kingdom of God in Israel. He would fulfil the scriptures and liberate God’s people, as Moses had freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Third, the Essenes at Qumran, with their exclusive and extreme outlook, expected a priestly messiah, associated with Aaron and the tribe of Levi. He would herald a great war in which God’s enemies would be vanquished and members of their sect vindicated.
(b) Jesus was not the messiah people expected. He brought a new interpretation: the messiah ushers in the Kingdom of God through a life of love and service and eventual death. He was anxious not to be identified with the Davidic or priestly ideas, and although he showed some affinity with the prophetic messiah, his idea of the Kingdom was very different. In Mark 8:31 he taught that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed and rise after three days.

Priestly - Essenes/Qumran, great war, Aaron/Levi. (b) 8 marks: very good 7-8, good 4-6, fair 0-3. May refer to: love, service and death; Kingdom of God; not political liberator; avoided Davidic/priestly; Mark 8:31 suffering Son of Man.

rows.prompt: ‘Jesus was aware of himself as the Messiah.’ Discuss this statement, referring to evidence from the gospels.
rows.model_answer: Jesus would have known the hopes of the people of Israel, especially those in Palestine. In his preaching, teaching and living he announced the Kingdom of God and showed awareness of himself as the Messiah in the sense of the one who heralded this kingdom. In John 4:25-26 the woman at the well says, ‘I know that Messiah is coming,’ and Jesus replies, ‘I am he, the one who is speaking to you.’ His acts of healing, love and compassion also show he knew what was expected of the Messiah. In Mark 14:3 an unnamed woman in the house of Simon the leper at Bethany anointed his head with costly nard, recognising him as Messiah. Jesus defended her, saying she had anointed his body beforehand for burial. However, Jesus was careful. He avoided the Davidic and priestly ideas, and the gospels show he was reluctant to be typecast as messiah by disciples or opponents, because in that political climate he would have to abandon his inclusive vision or be rejected as an impostor. In Mark 8:31 he openly taught that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and rise again. Scholars still debate how far he saw himself this way, because the gospels were written after the Resurrection.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: awareness of Israel’s hopes; announced the Kingdom; John 4:25-26 ‘I am he’; healing, love, compassion; Mark 14:3-9 anointing at Bethany and burial; reluctance to be typecast; impostor/political liberator; Mark 8:31 Son of Man; Jesus of history/Christ of faith debate. Must use gospel evidence for marks above fair.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by the ‘Jesus of history’ and the ‘Christ of faith’.
rows.model_answer: The ‘Jesus of history’ refers to Jesus as he actually lived before his death, sometimes called the ‘Pre-Easter Jesus’. The ‘Christ of faith’ refers to Jesus as understood by believers after the Resurrection, sometimes called the ‘Post-Easter Jesus’. The debate arises because all the gospels and New Testament accounts were written after the Resurrection. Scholars therefore ask what we can know about the historical Jesus, and to what extent the experience of the Resurrection and the early Christian community ‘coloured’ the evangelists’ view of him. This affects questions such as how far Jesus was aware of himself as the Messiah or ‘anointed one’, which scripture scholars have discussed for some time.
rows.marking_scheme: Jesus of history explained 3 marks; Christ of faith explained 3 marks; why the debate arises (gospels written post-Easter, Resurrection may have coloured the accounts) 4 marks.

rows.prompt: Why did Jesus not want to be seen simply as the Messiah that first-century Jews expected? Explain your answer.
rows.model_answer: First-century Palestine was a highly politicised place. Jews hoped and prayed for a messiah to deliver them from the pagan Romans, a new King David who would begin a new era. The Pharisees hoped for a prophetic messiah to free them from Roman rule, and the Essenes expected a priestly messiah who would lead a great war. These were political and sometimes violent hopes. Jesus’ agenda was not that of a political liberator. His understanding of Israel’s hopes was more inclusive, and he saw the messiah as one who ushers in the Kingdom of God through love, service and eventual death. If he had accepted the popular role, he would have had to abandon his own vision or be rejected as an impostor. So all the Gospels show his reluctance when disciples or opponents typecast him as messiah. In Mark 8:31 he corrected their ideas, teaching openly that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed and after three days rise again.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: politicised atmosphere; hope of freedom from Rome; Davidic, prophetic and priestly ideas; not a political liberator; inclusive vision; impostor; love, service, death; reluctance when typecast by disciples or opponents; Mark 8:31.
